                                      Abstract
          We give quantitative bounds on the sparsity of a real polynomial with
      non-negative coefficients vanishing on a slice of the Boolean cube {±1}n .
      We obtain similar bounds on the dimension of real orthogonal represen-
      tations of (the complement of) Johnson-type graphs. The estimates are
      related to the classical problem about coloring of Rn , as well as the ex-
      istence of error-correcting codes. We also give a simple combinatorial
      application to k-fold Hadamard matrices.


1    Introduction
A classical problem about coloring of Rn asks what is the minimum number
χ(Rn ) of colors needed to color Rn so that no two points of distance one share
the same color. It is easy to see that χ(Rn ) is finite. Furthermore, Larman and
Rogers have shown it can be bounded as χ(Rn ) ≤ 2O(n) [14]. An exponential
lower bound χ(Rn ) ≥ 2Ω(n) was proved by Frankl and Wilson in [5]. It is open to
determine the function χ(Rn ) exactly. A similar problem has been investigated
in the case of the sphere Srn−1 ⊆ Rn of radius r. In this setting, Raigorodskii
has shown that χ(Srn−1 ) grows exponentially with n for any fixed r > 1/2 [21]
(see also [20] and references within).
    Both the lower bounds of Frankl-Wilson and Raigorodskii proceed by lower-
bounding the chromatic number of a finite combinatorial graph embedded in
Rn or Srn−1 , respectively. In the case of [5], the graph is the Johnson graph
J(n, t, ℓ) whose vertices are t-element subsets of n-element universe, and they
are connected with an edge iff their intersection has size ℓ.
    In this paper, we consider orthogonal representations of Johnson-type graphs.
A (real) orthogonal representation of a graph G is a map ψ which assigns to
every vertex v a non-zero vector ψ(v) ∈ Rm so that ψ(v) and ψ(v ′ ) are orthog-
onal whenever v ̸= v ′ are not adjacent in G. The smallest m for which such

Orthogonal representations were introduced in the seminal paper of Lovász [16].
Representations of combinatorial Kneser-type graphs were studied by Haviv in
[7]. We will prove exponential lower bounds on the dimension of real orthog-
onal representations of (the complement of) of Johnson-type graphs, such as
J(2n, n, ℓ) with a suitable ℓ. A specific application to the coloring of Rn is
the following: suppose that ψ : Rn → Rm \ {0} is a map such that for ev-
ery x, y ∈ Rn of distance one, ψ(x) and ψ(y) are orthogonal. Then m grows
exponentially with n.
    The graphs we consider are graphs over the vertex set {±1}n where two
distinct x, y are connected if and and only if their Hadamard product, x ◦ y,
lies outside some prescribed set S ⊆ {±1}n . They can also be thought of as
Cayley graphs over the group Zn2 . It turns out that one can obtain orthogonal
representation for such graphs from polynomials f (x) with real, non-negative
coefficients that vanish when x ∈ S. The dimension of such a representation is
precisely the number of non-zero coefficients in f (x).
    This leads us to the following question regarding the sparsity of polynomials
with non-negative coefficients. Suppose f ∈ R≥0 [x1 , . . . , xn ] is a non-trivial
polynomial with non-negative coefficients which vanishes on a prescribed subset
S ⊆ {±1}n . How many non-zero coefficients must f contain? We give some
generic bounds for this problem. In Theorem 1, we show that f must contain
exponentially many non-zero coefficients in the specific case of S being a slice
of the hypercube. The statement is reminiscent of the Hegedus lemma [8, 23].
It is also related to error-correcting codes (cf. Section 3.2). In Section 3.3,
we will give combinatorial applications of Theorem 1 to generalized Hadamard
matrices.
    The above question is also related to problems in Fourier analysis of func-
tions on the Boolean cube {±1}n of an independent interest. A polynomial
f ∈ R[x1 , . . . , xn ] as above, can be regarded as a function f : {±1}n → R.
Then, the coefficients of the polynomial are precisely the Fourier coefficients of
the function. Our lower bound on the sparsity of f is, after a suitable normal-
ization,  a lower bound on the ℓ1 -norm of the Fourier spectrum of f given by

5     Open problems
We end the play with some open problems.
Problem 1. Show that dimR (J(n, 3, 1)) ≥ Ω(n2 ).

Problem 2. Let S be the union of {±1}nk over all 0 < k ≤ n divisible by 4.
Determine dimC (GS ) or dimR (GS ).
Problem 3. Given δ ∈ [0, 1), let cδ be the infimum c such that there exists a
map is in Corollary 3 part (i) with m ≤ O(2cn ). Then c0 = 0 and the Corollary
shows that cδ > 0 if δ > 0. Is it the case that limδ→0+ cδ = 0?

    Some comments are in order. In Problem 1, the trivial bounds are

                           Ω(n) ≤ dimR (J(n, 3, 1)) ≤ O(n2 ) .

Over complex numbers, one has dimC (J(n, 3, 1)) ≤ n+1. In contrast, dimF (J(n, 3, 1)) ≥
Ω(n2 ) over a field of characteristic two. In Problem 2, one has the bound
dimF (GS ) ≥ Ω(2n/2 ) over any field. This follows from the observation that GS
contains a clique of size2 Ω(2n/2 ). Over complex numbers, an upper bound
dimC (GS ) ≤ O(2cn ) with some constant c < 1 can be proved as in [10]. The
correct value of the constant is unknown. Over R, no such non-trivial upper
bound is known.
